summary: Defines the model and generic mechanisms for encapsulating Internet packets such as IPv4 and IPv6 inside IPv6 packets. This lets traffic cross parts of a network that handle only one kind of packet. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 tunneling carries an original packet inside a new IPv6 packet between two endpoints. The receiving endpoint removes the outer headers and continues forwarding the original packet.

subtitle: How an IPv6 packet can carry another packet between two tunnel endpoints.

tldr.problem: A network may need to carry selected packets across an IPv6 path or direct them through a chosen route without changing the original packet protocol.
tldr.mechanism: A tunnel entry point adds an IPv6 header, and optionally extension headers. The exit point removes those headers and forwards the original packet.
tldr.outcome: The tunnel appears as a virtual link to its endpoints. The RFC also defines controls for nested tunnels, packet sizes, and relaying errors.

today: RFC 2473 is a Proposed Standard published in December 1998. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What IPv6 Tunneling Does
sections.content:
IPv6 tunneling carries an original packet as the payload of another IPv6 packet. The new packet is called a tunnel packet, and the path it follows is the tunnel. The RFC describes tunneling IPv6 and IPv4 packets and says the model can also carry other protocol packets.

A typical use is for an intermediate node to select a forwarding path for particular packets. It adds IPv6 headers that identify the tunnel endpoints and guide the packet through that path.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel carries one packet inside an IPv6 packet between two nodes. This lets the network route the outer packet while preserving the original packet inside.

sections.title: The Tunnel Endpoints
sections.content:
An IPv6 tunnel acts as a virtual point-to-point link between its entry point and exit point. The entry point encapsulates an original packet and sends the tunnel packet. The exit point removes the tunnel headers and forwards the original packet toward its destination.

A tunnel carries packets in one direction. Two tunnels with opposite directions provide two-way communication. The RFC focuses on unicast endpoints but says the mechanisms also apply when the exit point uses an anycast or multicast address.
sections.plainLanguage: The entry point wraps a packet, and the exit point unwraps it. Each tunnel carries traffic one way, so two-way communication uses a tunnel in each direction.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
sections.content:
Encapsulation prepends an IPv6 header and may prepend extension headers to the original packet. The outer header names the entry point as its source and the exit point as its destination. Intermediate nodes process the outer packet using IPv6 rules.

At the exit point, IPv6 processes the extension headers in order. When the Next Header field identifies a tunnel protocol, the tunnel engine removes the outer headers and passes the original packet to the protocol named there. The node's routing table determines whether the tunnel link is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The entry point adds outer headers that direct the packet to the exit point. The exit point removes them and passes the original packet onward.

sections.title: Limiting Nested Tunnels
sections.content:
A tunnel packet can enter another tunnel, creating nested encapsulation. Each layer adds headers and can increase fragmentation. The RFC defines the Tunnel Encapsulation Limit option in a Destination Options header to limit how many additional tunnel levels a packet may enter.

The option type is 4 and its data length is one octet. An entry point checks the option before encapsulating: if the limit is zero, it discards the packet and sends an ICMP Parameter Problem; if nonzero, it carries the option forward with the value reduced by one. The recommended default limit is 4.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new tunnel adds another outer header. The Encapsulation Limit option counts how many more tunnel layers are allowed and stops the packet when the limit is reached.

sections.title: Packet Size and Error Reporting
sections.content:
Adding tunnel headers can make a packet exceed the tunnel MTU. The entry point handles fragmentation according to whether the original packet is IPv6 or IPv4 and, for IPv4, whether the Don't Fragment bit is set. Intermediate IPv6 nodes do not fragment forwarded tunnel packets; the exit point reassembles fragments before decapsulation.

An error detected inside a tunnel first reaches the tunnel entry point. That node relays the error to the source of the original packet. For nested tunnels, each inner entry point relays the error to the next outer entry point.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnel headers take up space, so a packet may need fragmentation or an error response. The entry point relays problems inside the tunnel back to the original sender.
